rv.q: The power of the play lies in its depiction of Kyle's efforts to gain a secure foothold for himself while safely maintaining a fully intact memory of Zoe; both are in jeopardy throughout.
Instead, it prefers to plunge directly into it, delivering dialogue which is at its most engaging when the ugly face of suffering is thrust up to the audience without mercy.
It is a completely enthralling show.
Dramatic focus and entirely believable points of conflict make this slow-moving story grab hold for its full two hours.
The splendid cast consists of Pete McElligott (Kyle), whose subtle, nuanced, always interesting performance is prize-worthy.
While Touch will not be for everyone, it is an impressive document of the workings of the human heart.
Problems aside, “Touch” remains a quietly involving piece about the human heart and the ways people respond in times of grief.
